They are the worst of creation.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who believed and did righteous deeds, they are the best of creation.﴾ ﴿Their reward with their Lord is gardens of perpetual residence beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. In Kitab al-Tahrir, it is said to be Madani, and this is the view of the majority. Abu Salih related from Ibn ʿAbbas that it is Makki, and Yahya ibn Sallam chose this view.

When [the surah] mentioned the revelation of the Qur'an, and in the surah before it (﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾ [al-ʿAlaq: 1]), it mentions here that the disbelievers were not going to desist from what they were upon until the Messenger came to them, reciting to them what had been revealed to him of the purified pages, which he was commanded to recite. It divided the disbelievers here into People of the Book and people of association (shirk). Some readers read (wa-l-mushrikūna) in the nominative, as a conjunction with (alladhīna kafarū), while the majority read it in the genitive, as a conjunction with (ahl al-kitāb). The People of the Book are the Jews and Christians, and the polytheists are the idol-worshippers among the Arabs. Ibn ʿAbbas said: the People of the Book are the Jews who were in Yathrib, namely Qurayẓah, al-Naḍīr and Banu Qaynuqāʿ, and the polytheists were those in Mecca and its surroundings and in Medina and its surroundings.

Mujahid and others said: they were not going to desist from disbelief and misguidance until the clear evidence came to them. Al-Farra' and others said: they were not going to desist from recognizing the truth of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) and awaiting his command until the clear evidence came to them, and then they divided at that point. Al-Zamakhshari said: the disbelievers of both groups used to say before the mission: "We will not desist from what we are upon of our religion until the awaited Prophet is sent, who is written about in the Torah and the Gospel, and he is Muhammad (ﷺ)." So Allah related what they used to say. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: a third opinion, excellent in meaning, is suitable for the meaning of the verse: that the intended sense is, "These people were not left out of Allah's command, power and care for them until Allah sends to them a warning Messenger by whom the proof is established against them and through whom He completes His blessing upon those who believe." It is as if He said: "They were not to be left neglected (sudan)." There are parallels to this in the Book of Allah, the Exalted. Ended.

It is also said: the meaning is "They were not going to be separated from their lives so that they would die until the clear evidence came to them." The apparent meaning is: "they were not going to be separated," i.e., some of them were not going to be detached from others, but each of them was affirming the other in what he had chosen for himself: this one in his belief concerning his law, and that one in his belief concerning his idols. The meaning is that their affection was connected and their word united until the clear evidence came to them.

It is also said: the meaning of (munfakkīn) is "perishing," from the saying: "the joints of the woman were dislocated at childbirth" (infakka ṣila al-mar'ah), i.e., they separated and did not reunite. The meaning is: "They were not going to be punished or perish except after the establishment of proof against them by the sending of Messengers and the revelation of Books." Ended. Some grammarians said it is the defective (nāqiṣah) verb, and (munfakkīn) is to be understood as "knowing the affair of Muhammad (ﷺ)" or something similar. The predicate of kāna and its sisters may not be omitted, either by restriction or by abbreviation; our companions have affirmed this, and they have a reason for prohibiting it which they mention in the science of grammar. They said, regarding the line (ḥīna laysa mujīr), meaning "in this world," that omitting the predicate there is a poetic necessity.

(Al-bayyinah) means the magnificent proof.

The majority read (rasūlun) in the nominative, as a substitute (badal) for (al-bayyinah). Ubayy and ʿAbd Allah read it in the accusative, as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of (al-bayyinah). ﴿Reciting purified pages﴾, i.e., parchments (qarāṭīs), purified (muṭahharah) from falsehood. ﴿Within which are scriptures﴾, i.e., written texts, ﴿upright﴾, straight, speaking the truth.

He also said: he singled out the People of the Book, meaning in the phrase (p-499) ﴿those who were given the Book did not divide﴾ after they had been mentioned together with the polytheists. It is possible that its original form had hamzah, which was then eased by substitution and assimilation; and it is possible that it derives from al-biraʾ, which is dust. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: this derivation makes the hamzah an error, and it is an unacceptable derivation, meaning deriving al-bariyyah without hamzah from al-bura (dust). The judgment upon the disbelievers of both groups is their eternal abiding in the Fire and their being the worst of creation. He began with the People of the Book, because they used to criticize his prophethood, and their offense is greater because they denied him while knowing about him. "The worst of creation" apparently has a general sense. It was said: "the worst of creation" refers to those who were contemporaries of the Messenger (ﷺ), since it is not far-fetched that among the disbelieving nations there were those worse than these, such as Pharaoh and the one who hamstrung the camel of Salih. The majority read ﴿the best of creation﴾ as the counterpart of ﴿the worst of creation﴾; Hamid and ʿAmir ibn ʿAbd al-Wahid read khiyār al-bariyyah, the plural of khayyir, like jayyid and jiyād. The rest of the surah is clear, and its explanation has been given earlier, both singly and in composition.
